items.title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.original_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_description: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 16:09 Life insurers are AI. The next challenge is preparing for policyholders who use AI to understand, question and optimize their policies. November 5, 2026 Image Imagine the customer of a 20-year-old life insurance policy trying to figure out if it makes sense to surrender the policy. Do they call the insurance company first, hoping to talk to a knowledgeable agent? Probably not. They will upload the policy contract, riders and most recent statement to the AI assistant with a list of questions: What benefits would be lost by surrendering the policy? What happens to the outstanding loans? Are there other alternatives to surrendering the policy? Which policy provisions are the most important to consider before deciding? This AI might be right, or might be partly right, or might be very wrong. But what is becoming abundantly clear is that this customer arrives at their insurer with a level of analysis and a body of knowledge that once cost time, or cost money, or both. This leads me back to the question insurers have been asking for years about how AI will change what we do: underwriting, servicing, operations, all inside the enterprise. So what happens when the policyholder is AI-enabled as well? The information gap is starting to change The Society of Actuaries Research Institute is now seeking research on policyholder behavior in the artificial intelligence era. According to the proposal request, it is possible for consumers to use AI to understand a policy's provisions better to improve their premiums, loans and withdrawals, and claims through improved product features. That isn't proof that AI has changed lapse rates, loan behavior, or benefit usage yet. It's on the research agenda. The difference is significant. But the formal asking of such questions by the actuarial community indicates that consumer AI requires attention before the results become apparent in experience studies. Up until recently, this has created a bit of a predicament: an insurer has product specialists, actuaries, underwriters, policy administration systems, and decades of institutional knowledge; a policyholder has a lengthy contract written in technical language and maybe the occasion to review it a couple of times. Generative AI won't remove that imbalance entirely, but it certainly lowers the cost of asking sophisticated questions about a complex contract. That alone changes the dynamic of that interaction. A long-lived contract can meet a very different customer Life insurance is unique because the contract could go on for decades, and the technology available to the user would be different from the present one. A policy issued in the age of paper statements and telephone calls may one day be managed by a consumer carrying a persistence layer of AI that summarizes documents, compares alternatives, remembers every previous conversation, and prepares detailed questions before every interaction. The policy's bones haven't altered one bit. But a policyholder's ability to kick the tires and check them out has. All this matters because many decisions and actions can occur throughout the lifecycle of a single life insurance policy: premium payment policy, loans, withdrawals, changes of beneficiary, conversion, surrender, and more. By making those decisions easier to understand and execute throughout the life of the product, there's no guarantee that customer behavior in the future will continue to be like the historical behaviors that informed product assumptions. Policyholder behavior may become an AI issue SOA's current research request explicitly identifies potential effects on lapses, loans, withdrawals, and benefit usage. A separate 2026 SOA call for essays on AI and the potential for antiselection in life insurance distribution asks whether AI could help applicants or intermediaries anticipate underwriting outcomes, compare carriers, select underwriting pathways and apply sophisticated placement strategies at greater scale. Once more, these are questions under investigation, not established outcomes. But, one thing appears clear: certain presumptions in life insurance are based on how people behave. Making it easier to evaluate the timing and consequences of a lapse, loan, withdrawal, conversion, surrender, or benefit election changes behavior in ways that historical behavior doesn't predict. The negative reaction to that realization is to predict material disruption. The right reaction is to begin measuring whether AI-assisted behavior is emerging, where it's concentrated, and if it's big enough to matter. From a more strategic perspective, for our actuarial and product teams, consumer AI could one day become another behavioral variable to study, rather than just a way to service customers better. AI-enabled policyholders can also be good for insurers This should not be framed only as a new risk. When a customer understands the policy, it allows them to ask the right questions, know what benefits they have, prepare the right documents, and know what decision they are making. Beneficiaries will use AI to organize materials for a claim, point out relevant policy language, and understand what the insurer is asking for. A policyholder who walks up to the window to service their policy will know the difference between a loan, withdrawal, and a surrender. This is consistent with the financial services research. In July 2026, LIMRA reported that AI is increasingly being studied not only as a tool that assists advisors but as a potential source of analysis and financial guidance directly to consumers. While more knowledgeable buyers are good for insurers, they also bring heightened expectations. A customer who has just received an instantaneous explanation of a policy provision may be less patient about waiting for days to get a generic response from a service agent. The customer's AI is not the insurer's AI Yet there is a boundary—the policyholder's AI is outside of the insurer's control. The model was not chosen, trained, fed, or even provided with its system prompt by the insurer. Your AI could be reading an outdated contract, skipping an endorsement, not grasping a rider, getting guaranteed vs. non-guaranteed values mixed up, or just making up a provision out of whole cloth that does not exist. The assertion could be false, or at least inaccurate. The enterprise response is to make verifying what the authoritative policy information says more accessible. Suppose a customer says, "My AI says this rider gives me a different option." It should be easy for a service person to say, "Let's review what your current contract and its effective endorsements, transaction history, and applicable rules say about this." The more external AI becomes part of customer decision-making, the more valuable clear, accessible, and authoritative policy context becomes. Soon, the customer may send the AI instead The next step is not difficult to imagine: the policyholder does not merely use AI before contacting the insurer. The AI contacts the insurer. That scenario is beginning to appear in insurance discussions already. An October 2026 Insurance Thought Leadership article described consumer AI agents calling insurers and other businesses on behalf of users. At the same time, NIST is developing work around identity and authorization for software and AI agents as agent-to-agent interactions move from concept toward practical infrastructure. This brings us to a much bigger question for life insurers: what if a chatbot does work? How would your service channel know that it's talking to software working for a policyholder? What data could be returned through that channel? What happens when a customer AI and your system don't agree on a policy provision? When does it become important to switch the interaction over to a person? There's nothing in those two scenarios that necessitates banning the use of AI in customer service. It just means that we, as users of these services, will need to create different channels for them to go through. Build policyholder AI readiness Insurers do not need to predict exactly how fast consumer agents will mature, but they do need to prepare for the direction of travel. First, make authoritative policy context easier to retrieve and explain. A policyholder's AI will only be as useful as the documents and information it can access. Clear digital contracts, current riders, transaction history, and understandable definitions reduce the chance that outside AI starts from incomplete context. Next, test servicing journeys with customers being assisted by AI in mind. When customers arrive having 10 specific questions, they should not follow the same process as someone who has only general questions. Third, watch how behavior changes. Teams — actuarial, product, servicing — that rely on lapses, loans, withdrawals, conversions, benefit usage, and channel usage need to understand what constitutes a significant deviation. We want to avoid blaming AI if another force is at work. The goal is to build evidence that indicates that AI is a cause before rewriting our assumptions about behavior. Fourth, prepare digital channels for external agents. Identity, consent, disclosure and escalation will become practical. We do not want to automatically trust an outside agent. We do want to ensure legitimate customer assistance can reach us and not diminish customer protection. The next AI transformation may happen outside the insurer When asked about the insurance AI strategy, carriers invariably identify the same things: automated underwriting, automated servicing, automated claims, automated document processing, and automated decision support. However, when it comes to the impact of artificial intelligence on enhancing service innovation, customer capabilities are also affected. The increased understanding could allow them to compare things to other products, which could open them up to asking difficult questions. However, what I think we have not talked about and probably is an elephant in the room is that insurers are not going to be in control of all this. They can only prepare for it. Will the next phase of life insurance AI be defined by how intelligent the insurer becomes? Or by what happens when the policyholder becomes intelligent at machine speed? Bhargavi Vepuri

items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.summary: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.extracted_text: Terror Suit Against Drugmakers Draws US Supreme Court Inquiry Article 0 Comments The U.S. Supreme Court asked the Trump administration for input on an appeal from pharmaceutical and medical-device companies that are trying to stop a lawsuit accusing them of helping to finance terrorist attacks in Iraq. The companies are seeking review of a ruling that let American terrorism victims sue the companies for allegedly paying millions of dollars in bribes to secure medical-supply contracts with the Iraqi Ministry of Health from 2004 to 2013. The victims say the money went to Jaysh al-Mahdi, a militant group that controlled the ministry. The lawsuit names units of AstraZeneca Plc, Roche Holding Ltd., GE HealthCare Technologies Inc., Johnson & Johnson, Pfizer Inc. and Viatris Inc. as defendants. The companies were sued by servicemembers and civilians who served in Iraq, as well as their families. The justices directed their request Monday to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top Supreme Court lawyer. The companies say they contracted with the ministry at the encouragement of the U.S. government. They told the Supreme Court that, even if true, the allegations against them weren’t sufficient to let a lawsuit go forward under the U.S. Anti-Terrorism Act. The drugmakers said the suit didn’t allege a sufficiently close connection between their transactions with the ministry and specific acts of terrorism. The companies also contended the law requires a showing that a defendant intended to help a terror attack succeed. In urging the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, the victims said the companies knew their bribes financed attacks and yet continued paying for years. A federal appeals court in Washington ruled the suit could go forward, saying the complaint adequately alleged that the companies repeatedly structured their transactions in an unusual and illegal manner that facilitated Jaysh al-Mahdi’s activities. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in 2023 that the Anti-Terrorism Act couldn’t be used to hold social media companies responsible for a 2017 shooting in an Istanbul nightclub. Both sides in the Iraq case contended the court’s reasoning in the 2023 case supported their arguments. The case is AstraZeneca U.K. v. Atchley , 26-245. items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

No longer enough to move the needle: Bowen, Gallagher Re - Artemis.bm Insured catastrophe losses surpass $100bn in 2026. No longer enough to move the needle: Bowen, Gallagher Re 10th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Global insured catastrophe losses have now surpassed the $100 billion level in 2026, according to Steve Bowen, Chief Science Officer at reinsurance broker Gallagher Re. This marks the 10th consecutive year in which the threshold has been exceeded on an inflation-adjusted basis, and the seventh consecutive year on a nominal basis. Gallagher Re recently reported that natural catastrophe insured losses had reached $92 billion between January and September 2026, marking the lowest total for the first nine months of the year since 2019, and 29% below the 10-year average of $128 billion. Insured catastrophe losses in 2025 reached the $100 billion threshold by September. Once again, in 2026 the industry has experienced the $100 billion of insured catastrophe loss total in advance of the end of the year. In a recent LinkedIn post, Bowen explained that the industry has seen a dramatic shift in how the global insurance market reacts to annual losses exceeding $100 billion. “A decade ago, this was a huge deal. Today, it is notable, but no longer enough on its own to move the needle,” Bowen said. He continued: “The industry has learned important lessons from some difficult and highly impactful loss years. Better risk management, stronger capital positions, improved modeling, and more disciplined pricing have left the market in a much stronger position to absorb these higher loss costs.” The Chief Science Officer importantly turned attention to how the market will react when annual insured losses surpass $200 billion on a nominal basis for the first time In fact, with the most recent five-year nominal average standing at roughly $150 billion, losses reaching $200 billion increasingly looks like a matter of when, rather than if. All of which makes the build-up of industry capital and capacity increasingly more important. Along with further innovation in resilience and risk transfer, as protection gaps across the globe increasingly continue to expand. Also as the frequency and severity of secondary perils continues to rise, especially severe convective storms, pressure on the re/insurance industry will only intensify. All of which should turn more companies towards the capital markets to obtain efficient protection. Bowen concludes: “Climate risk cannot simply be viewed through the lens of expected insured losses. The societal implications are much broader. The countries and communities most vulnerable to climate risk are often those with the fewest resources available to protect themselves ahead of time or recover in the aftermath. “The insurance and broader financial sectors have an important role to play. That means not only working to narrow the protection gap, but helping build greater climate resilience through new funding mechanisms, innovative risk-transfer solutions, better risk assessment information, and greater investment in adaptation. “A more resilient insurance industry matters. The arrangement, a first of its kind in Canada, applies parametric financing to the charitable […] Munich Re teams with Wawanesa & WWF-Canada to launch parametric river flood solution was published by: www.Artemis.bm Our catastrophe bond deal directory Sign up for our free weekly email newsletter here .
items.extracted_text: Munich Re teams with Wawanesa & WWF-Canada to launch parametric river flood solution - Artemis.bm Munich Re teams with Wawanesa & WWF-Canada to launch parametric river flood solution - Artemis.bm Munich Re teams with Wawanesa & WWF-Canada to launch parametric river flood solution 10th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Reinsurance firm Munich Re has partnered with Wawanesa and World Wildlife Fund Canada (WWF-Canada), to develop and launch a parametric river flood insurance solution that will deliver rapid funding to safeguard nature-based restoration across the Wolastoq (Saint John River) watershed. The arrangement, a first of its kind in Canada, applies parametric financing to the charitable sector to ensure climate resilience investments are protected and sustained over time. The parametric arrangement was developed with support from Munich Re Canada, alongside climate-peril expertise from reinsurance broker Marsh Re. Under the parametric structure, Wawanesa funding will be triggered by independently measured river levels, and if predetermined river conditions are met, Wawanesa will provide up to $1 million in funding each year, capped at a maximum of $3 million over a three-year period, to WWF-Canada. Home to more than 500,000 people and stretching nearly 700 kilometres from Quebec to the Bay of Fundy, the Wolastoq watershed has experienced repeated major flooding and high-water events over recent decades. This initiative will help support WWF-Canada and local partners in assessing impacts and responding more quickly to flood events, helping protect years of restoration investment from climate-related setbacks. The funds will also support post-event assessments, targeted remediation, and local partner mobilisation, and continued restoration work, helping bridge the critical period following a significant high-water event before conventional public or charitable aid arrives. Munich Re explained that this initiative brings together a shared commitment to climate resilience and community impact with company’s expertise in parametric solutions and natural catastrophe risk. “At the heart of the solution is a parametric structure linked to observed river levels, demonstrating how risk-transfer innovation can help address climate-related challenges and strengthen community resilience. It is a great example of what can happen when insurance expertise, climate science and a shared sense of purpose come together,” Munich Re said. James Bond, SVP, Chief Legal & Strategy Officer of Wawanesa, commented: “Resilience means investing before disaster strikes – and making sure that work can continue after it does. This innovative approach brings financial innovation and community investment together to help sustain restoration and resilience efforts already underway across the Wolastoq watershed. It is a practical example of how insurers can help communities support long-term resilience and reduce risk over time.” In addition, the initiative also builds on Wawanesa’s existing commitment to the region, having invested over $1 million with WWF-Canada in the Wolastoq watershed over the past three years through its Climate Champions program. Local projects include restoring floodplains, stabilising riverbanks and planting native trees and shrubs, all of which effectively helps natural systems slow and absorb floodwater while creating long-term resilience benefits for communities throughout the watershed. Alex Portman, Head of Corporate Partnerships at WWF-Canada, said: “The restoration of a 230-metre section of the Rivière-à-la-Truite near Edmundston is one example of how local partners are building resilience through nature-based solutions. Because this work takes years to deliver results, major floods can put hard-won progress at risk. This innovative partnership could help local organizations quickly access funding when it’s needed most, safeguarding restoration investments and keeping projects moving forward.” Furthermore, both Wawanesa and WWF-Canada said that they see the partnership as a potential model for how finance and risk-transfer tools can complement investment in climate adaptation and resilience, supporting not only recovery after disruptive events but also the long-term resilience benefits created through nature-based solutions. While the project will initially just focus on the Wolastoq watershed, the partners plan to evaluate lessons learned from the rollout to assess whether the initiative and similar parametric approaches could support resilience and restoration across other regions in Canada. Mitchell McEwen, Director, Sustainability, Climate Resilience & Community Impact at Wawanesa, added: “This model shows how risk-transfer expertise can provide greater speed and certainty for local climate resilience projects. items.extracted_text: ILS expansion beyond cat must be driven by pricing, structure, understanding: Doris, Twelve Securis - Artemis.bm ILS expansion beyond cat must be driven by pricing, structure, understanding: Doris, Twelve Securis - Artemis.bm ILS expansion beyond cat must be driven by pricing, structure, understanding: Doris, Twelve Securis 10th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard While the ILS market has moved beyond traditional property catastrophe risk and expanded into emerging perils such as cyber, casualty and specialty lines in recent years, Cahal Doris of Twelve Securis has expressed that this growth must be driven by pricing, structure and understanding, and not simply for the sake of expanding the market. Speaking to Artemis around the reinsurance conference season, Doris, who serves as Chief Investment Officer ILS at the firm, outlined that Twelve Securis views the current ILS market as being very healthy. However, he also stressed that the market’s resilience will always be tested following any major loss event. “We would describe the market as very healthy. The cat bond market has continued to set records – in terms of issuance but also outstanding market with new sponsors entering the market,” Doris explained. “Nevertheless, a healthy market is not simply one that grows. Ultimately, its resilience will be tested following a major loss event. Managers and investors therefore need to remain focused on liquidity, collateral management and portfolio construction even during favourable conditions.” As highlighted, in recent years, the ILS market has expanded from traditional property cat risk and tapped into expanding perils such as casualty, cyber and specialty lines. However, it’s important to remember that while interest and issuance is growing, these non-peak sectors still represent a small fraction of the overall ILS market. All of which leads Doris to highlight the importance that comes with expanding into these perils. “We remain positive about innovation beyond natural catastrophe risk, but expansion should not happen simply for the sake of expanding the ILS universe,” Doris stressed. He continued: “The fundamental question is whether a risk can be understood, priced and structured in a way that provides investors with adequate compensation. That is particularly important for longer-tail risks, where investors must accept significantly different liquidity characteristics from traditional cat bonds.” In regard to cyber, Doris said that the peril remains particularly challenging given that it is a dynamic, man-made risk where historical data and traditional catastrophe modelling approaches have limitations, which leads the CIO to state that this view has been reinforced further through the advances that have been made with AI in recent years. “Casualty presents a different challenge: its long-tail nature makes ultimate losses and reserve development significantly more difficult to assess. Broadly, investors will view short-tail natural catastrophe risk in a different allocation bucket to longer tail lines,” Doris added. Given the ILS market’s rapid expansion in recent years, a number of challenges continue to exist within the space. One of which Doris observes centres around maintaining underwriting and investment discipline as competition for risk increases off the back of successive positive years. The CIO also added that strong capital inflows can encourage investors to move further down the risk spectrum, leading him to say that “a clear communication channel with investors is necessary to allow managers to control risk while targeting suitable returns.” Doris continued: “A second structural challenge remains the industry’s broad reliance on third-party catastrophe models. Most participants ultimately work from a relatively concentrated set of model assumptions. We believe managers need an independent view of risk that challenges those assumptions and incorporates evolving factors such as climate change.” Highlighting key considerations that investors should be examining when deploying ILS capital, the Twelve Securis CIO emphasises that as the market continues to grow, investors should be looking beyond gaining access to transactions, given that access alone is becoming less of a differentiator. “The key questions are whether a manager has the resources and expertise to develop an independent view of risk whether it can process a significantly larger opportunity set without compromising investment discipline and whether its interests are genuinely aligned with those of its investors,” Doris told Artemis. He concluded: “Scale is valuable when it supports deeper analytics, technology, operational resilience and access across different segments of the market. But scale by itself is not enough. Investors should assess how those capabilities translate into portfolio construction and, ultimately, risk-adjusted performance.” Read all of our interviews with ILS market and reinsurance sector professionals here . items.rss_title: Top UK Regulator Says Banks Are Trimming AI Risk as Alarm Grows
items.rss_description: UK banks have begun trimming exposure to artificial intelligence as alarm mounts about a brutal correction in the sector, according to the Bank of England’s top supervisor. In her first interview since taking over the Prudential Regulation Authority in July, …
items.extracted_text: Top UK Regulator Says Banks Are Trimming AI Risk as Alarm Grows Article 0 Comments UK banks have begun trimming exposure to artificial intelligence as alarm mounts about a brutal correction in the sector, according to the Bank of England’s top supervisor. In her first interview since taking over the Prudential Regulation Authority in July, Katharine Braddick said the BOE’s extensive interrogation of banks’ AI exposure hasn’t shown that lenders would be an “amplifier” of any AI shock. Still, the central bank isn’t being complacent. “We’re all alarmed at the moment, aren’t we?” she said, though the BOE is not currently planning to use capital rules to encourage lower exposures. Banks are “all asking themselves that question” of whether to reduce exposure, she said of a retrenchment she’s seen recently. “I can see firms looking at their risk appetite and thinking and considering, ‘Yes this client, not that client.’ You do see it feed through.” A potential AI implosion has been just one of the many things keeping Braddick on her toes since she became the first outsider to take over the 13-year-old PRA, a cornerstone of Britain’s post-financial crisis infrastructure. Braddick joined the authority a few months after Anthropic PBC’s Mythos model spooked watchdogs and governments across the world, forcing them to contemplate unprecedented cyberattacks perpetrated by agentic AI. More recently, the US midterm elections drove a sell off in AI-related stocks, causing a rout that’s already imperiled Anthropic’s much-anticipated public offering. Braddick, a Cambridge University graduate who spent almost two decades in policy before a three-year stint at Barclays Plc, says AI risks are “constant conversation.” Broader issues around operational resilience have also been of paramount concern in her conversations with bank chief executive officers so far. The PRA and Financial Conduct Authority will publish guidance later this month on how to deal with risks from frontier AI and quantum computing. Braddick said the approach would be “quite concrete,” including laying out governance expectations, and hopes it will kick off an “iterative exercise” that will lead to deeper partnerships between the BOE and the industry. Braddick is also looking at how to operationalize the “minimum viable bank” framework proposed by BOE Governor Andrew Bailey earlier this year, a concept that would require banks to have “bare metal” functions capable of delivering continuous service in case of a cyber-attack. “It’s an urgent question,” Braddick said of deliberations on which banks should be required to have their own infrastructure, as well as how to create a structure for smaller lenders who can’t afford their own rails. No deadlines have been set for introducing such rules. This kind of resilience-focused work is “one of the most important things we can do for the UK’s competitiveness,” Braddick, a deputy governor of the BOE, said. “Operational resilience doesn’t deliver financial resilience. But the two are out of kilter, so we need to uplift operational resilience.” Case for Stability Still, capital requirements have taken center stage in the public debate on competitiveness, with banks leading demands for reprieves. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey recently wrote to Governor Bailey urging the BOE to implement agreed reforms “as quickly as possible” and deliver “further proposals” to keep the UK competitive. Braddick called Healey’s letter “completely understandable,” though it hadn’t changed her thinking on the PRA’s approach to capital. The regulator sits on the Financial Policy Committee, set to later this week discuss a package of capital reforms in the works, following last year’s decision to reduce the UK’s benchmark capital requirements by 1 percentage point to 13%. The outcome of the deliberations will be announced on Nov. 26. “I don’t have a defensive position on capital, but it is the keystone of everything that we do about financial resilience,” she said. She declined to go into specifics, such as on lowering the countercyclical buffer’s neutral level — the additional capital banks are required to hold in normal economic conditions — to below 2% or concentration risk charges. She said she doesn’t expect “further proposals” by Healey to lead to another grand package of reforms, instead arguing the case for stability and predictability after recent change. That philosophy is helping drive the PRA’s first five-year strategy she’s promised to deliver early next year. Braddick said her officials would “soon” begin testing some of its ideas on firms, particularly around how the authority should be held accountable for growth and competitiveness. The PRA has also promised more transparency, which Braddick said was partly informed by her time at Barclays when she realized how much of a mystery regulators can be from the outside. Banks have been pushing in particular for more transparency on a key capital buffer for so-called other systemic institutions, something that has long been a black box. “I recognize the general observation, which is that there are bits of our regime that are opaque to firms, where it’s useful for us to ask whether that opacity is necessary or even intended,” she said, adding that she was “open to that conversation.” Another conversation Braddick seems open to is with Swiss bank UBS Group AG, which has signaled it’s open to moving its headquarters if Switzerland pushes ahead with a new capital regime. Braddick said she hasn’t spoken to “a large Swiss bank about where it might want to headquarter” but she has heard from two different firms in recent weeks that have asked about relocating to the UK. “What UBS want to do is up to UBS,” she said. “We don’t chase business, but where firms are interested in what it means to locate in the UK, whether it works for them, we would always want to talk to them.” Photo: Katharine Braddick Photographer: Betty Laura Zapata/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: Measles Cases in Pennsylvania Now Surpass 1,500: State Health Department Article 0 Comments The number of measles cases in Pennsylvania reached 1,505 as of Monday, up 18 from the previous update on Friday, as the state battles its worst outbreak of the disease in years. The MRP coordinates documentation of the repairs necessary to return the structure to its preloss …
items.extracted_text: Same Goal, Different Pressures: Building Managed Repair Partnerships on Mutual Understanding Article 0 Comments The premise of managed repair is straightforward: rather than insurance carriers reimbursing policyholders directly for property damage, carriers refer claims to a managed repair program. The MRP coordinates documentation of the repairs necessary to return the structure to its preloss condition and, where selected by the property owner to effect those repairs, oversees repairs through a network of preapproved, vetted contractors. But as much as all stakeholders in the managed repair ecosystem share a common desire to restore policyholders’ homes, lives and businesses, the underlying concerns and priorities that each is grappling with can be worlds apart. As a third-party administrator, we have a vantage point on this disconnect — and on the importance of mitigating it. We know that the pressures contractors absorb today could show up tomorrow in cycle times, estimate accuracy and the policyholder experience. So, in the interest of increased understanding, we recently asked our network of insurance restoration professionals to share what’s really happening inside their businesses. The takeaway for property claims leaders is not just in what contractors told us, but in what their feedback may indicate about the challenges and opportunities ahead. Lance Malcolm Cost of Doing Business: The Defining Concern for Restoration Businesses Today Operating pressures, including project delays, cancellations, safety concerns and escalating insurance-related costs, were recurring themes throughout contractor feedback, with rising material costs, economic uncertainty and labor shortages topping contractors’ list of worries. Material costs especially stood out because concern about them was nearly identical in every U.S. region, emphasizing that this is an industrywide structural pressure rather than a short-term, geography-specific issue. None of these trends were particularly surprising given current headlines, but what’s interesting is how contractors are handling them. When asked how the labor market is affecting their pricing, 58% said they have absorbed higher labor costs to keep their prices steady, yet only about a third have raised prices on their jobs. That pattern holds in every region and at every firm size, from two-person outfits to shops with more than 100 employees. Although steady job pricing may sound like good news for carriers, the rising underlying costs contractors are facing create an increasingly unsustainable model for the managed repair ecosystem. If contractors continue to absorb higher operational expenses without corresponding pricing adjustments, the industry could see mounting labor challenges, longer project timelines, greater strain on the customer experience and increased pressure on contractor profitability. Over time, these dynamics may contribute to network contraction as some firms scale back operations or exit the market altogether. Impact of The Labor Market Can Be Felt Well Beyond Pricing Nearly nine in 10 (86%) insurance restoration contractors said the labor market is affecting their business. More than half find it harder to hire qualified workers, and a similar percentage report rising wage expectations. The effects extend well into contractors’ day-to-day operations. The most common result is longer job cycle times, followed by effects on pricing and their ability to scale projects. For claims leaders, the real concern here is cycle time, as faster repairs ultimately drive policyholder satisfaction. It’s worth noting that the labor market impacts felt by contractors vary by geography. Labor shortages are the top concern in the Northeast and Midwest but barely register in the Southwest and West, where economic uncertainty leads instead. The size of the firm matters too, as midsized firms with 26 to 75 employees are more than twice as likely as smaller firms to name safety and insurance pressures as their biggest concern. The question for the industry is how to create the flexibility needed to sustain a healthy managed repair ecosystem while continuing to drive consistency, estimate accuracy and customer outcomes. Managed repair stakeholders, including carriers, networks and contractors, each play an important role in controlling loss adjustment expense through disciplined documentation, transparent estimating practices and effective repair oversight. Absent that flexibility, contractors may increasingly pursue alternative business opportunities, reducing available network capacity and making it more difficult to deliver the estimating expertise, repair quality and policyholder experience carriers have come to expect. Increased Industry Collaboration Unsurprisingly, nearly every contractor we surveyed uses technology only eight of 473 said they don’t. The most common uses are cost estimation and scoping, communications and documentation, and project management. Contractors are also adopting tools in the field for drying and remediation, moisture detection, and damage assessment. This is encouraging. Estimation and documentation have historically been the points where carriers and contractors get stuck in back-and-forth. Shared digital workflows such as real-time photo documentation, live video and consistent estimating platforms can shorten review cycles, improve indemnity accuracy and cut the friction that frustrates adjusters and contractors alike. The industry is also seeing how technology can help bridge this gap. Solutions that improve estimate quality, accelerate review workflows, increase project visibility and leverage AI-assisted decision support are reducing friction across the claims and restoration process. Understanding Must be Followed by Action To strengthen the managed repair process, carriers must not only understand the burdens their restoration partners face but also collaborate on solutions that benefit the industry as a whole. We’ve taken the first step with the 2026 Managed Repair Market Report , but acknowledging the state of the industry can’t be the end of the story. Carriers and program partners must now use these insights to make smarter decisions for the future. Managed repair depends on effective coordination among carriers, contractors and policyholders. As carriers shape their future claims and vendor strategies, these market dynamics should be an important consideration in strategic planning to help preserve network capacity, sustain performance and continue delivering the customer experience policyholders expect. items.title: US sues Lyft, alleges discrimination against disabled riders
items.original_title: US sues Lyft, alleges discrimination against disabled riders
items.rss_title: US sues Lyft, alleges discrimination against disabled riders
items.rss_description: The U.S. Justice Department sued Lyft on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing ​services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.
items.extracted_text: Justice Department sued Lyft on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing ​services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs. The lawsuit seeks $53 million for individuals with disabilities whom Lyft allegedly discriminated against, and who have submitted complaints to Lyft or the Department of Justice, the DOJ said in a statement. Lyft said it disagreed with the allegations made in the Justice Department lawsuit that was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The lawsuit alleges Lyft violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which prohibits private transportation companies from discriminating based on disability. The lawsuit seeks a court order to force Lyft to stop the alleged discrimination, to modify its policies to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, and to train its staff and drivers on the law, the Justice Department said. The Justice Department alleged that Lyft and its drivers routinely refuse service to individuals with disabilities and refuse to reasonably modify Lyft’s policies and practices to avoid such discrimination. “We have long-standing policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” Lyft said in a statement responding to the lawsuit. Lyft also said it has cooperated with the DOJ during its review. Last year, the US government sued Uber, accusing the ride-sharing company of violating the same federal law by discriminating against passengers with disabilities. That lawsuit sought $125 million for individuals subjected to the alleged discrimination and who previously submitted complaints to Uber or the Justice Department. Uber had said it disagreed with all of the allegations and was committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities. items.title: Reinsurance renewal discussions shaped by abundant capital, loss concerns
items.original_title: Reinsurance renewal discussions shaped by abundant capital, loss concerns
items.rss_title: Reinsurance renewal discussions shaped by abundant capital, loss concerns
items.rss_description: Property reinsurance rates are expected to fall again at Jan. 1 renewals, with increased competition also giving cedents opportunities to negotiate broader coverage and more favorable terms, brokers say.
items.extracted_text: Gallagher & Co. , Howden , Lockton , Marsh Nov 10, 2026 BOSTON — Property reinsurance rates are expected to fall again at Jan. 1 renewals, with increased competition also giving cedents opportunities to negotiate broader coverage and more favorable terms, brokers say. Casualty reinsurance rates, meanwhile, are expected to remain relatively flat as reinsurers weigh ample capacity against persistent claims inflation and uncertainty around U.S. liability litigation, they said during interviews at the American Property Casualty Insurance Association annual conference in Boston, a major reinsurance renewal meeting for the U.S. market. Property reinsurance rate decreases at the January and midyear 2026 renewals were both slightly above 15% on a risk-adjusted basis, said Kyle Menendez, New York-based managing director and head of U.S. property for Howden Re. Similar reductions are expected at the upcoming renewals, he said. As in 2025, insurers and reinsurers have not faced major hurricane claims in 2026 so far. “Property rates are going to continue to go down,” said Laura Murphy, Minneapolis-based leader, North America property, Lockton Re. While some market participants suggest that declines will slow, “all of the influences that are driving the softening rate environment continue to exist,” she said. Competition at renewals is likely to increase, she said. Reinsurers are becoming increasingly competitive and modestly expanding their risk appetites to maintain their positions on programs, Ms. Murphy said. Capital supply and reinsurance demand are more closely balanced in the casualty market. “From a supply and demand perspective, we’ve seen general parity between the supply and demand for casualty reinsurance,” said Anthony DiLorenzo, Philadelphia-based U.S. casualty broking leader for Lockton Re. Although casualty reinsurance capital is adequate to plentiful, reinsurers remain concerned about the U.S. litigation environment and its effect on claims costs, said Brian Flasinski, Philadelphia-based CEO of Gallagher Re North America, a unit of Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. “Casualty is a bit more of a nuanced market because of the uncertainty around the U.S. liability,” Mr. Flasinski said. “The social inflation, litigation financing, nuclear verdicts — they’re all traits that don’t exist in a lot of places around the world.” While recent accident years have seen some “pretty material rate improvement” across the general, excess and umbrella liability, they are also showing signs of higher-than-average loss development, said Mike McCann, New York-based U.S. casualty product leader for Lockton Re. As loss costs rise, indications suggest primary casualty insurance rate increases may be slowing. “We’re starting to hear that the primary market is starting to moderate in terms of the level of rate increases,” said Chris Ross, New York-based global casualty leader at Marsh Re. Meanwhile, alternative capital, which has become an established source of capacity in property reinsurance, is attracting growing interest in the casualty sector. “There’s certainly an influx of third-party capital into the casualty space,” said Mr. DiLorenzo of Lockton Re. Cedents increasingly ask about alternative capital during discussions about casualty reinsurance, said Carrie Byler, New York-based managing director and head of U.S. casualty for Howden Re. “It’s definitely beginning to happen,” she said of alternative in casualty reinsurance. Program structures are changing in the softening property reinsurance market. 2026 renewals were “very much a discussion of rate change and rate reduction,” said David Duffy, New York-based global property leader for Marsh Re. The 2027 renewals will involve broader negotiations, he said. “There’s going to be a discussion around rate, and there will be rate reductions,” Mr. Duffy said. “There will also be a discussion around coverage and program structure.” “There’s a willingness to discuss terms as part of the broader conversation,” said Adam Schwebach, Tampa-based head of North American property for Gallagher Re. “Price is certainly a part of that conversation. Terms will be a part of that conversation, and coverage will be probably the most interesting part of that conversation. We’re seeing a willingness from the reinsurers to start to engage in more of those conversations,” Mr. Schwebach said. Potential changes include horizontal coverages for multiple events and aggregate coverage for many smaller, retained events, Mr. Schwebach said. Multi-year structure could also be part of discussions, he added. Reinsurers are more willing to provide frequency-related protection as part of an overall relationship, Mr. Duffy said. Discussions about coverage began in 2026 and have intensified, Gallagher Re’s Mr. Flasinski said. “I think the optionality is there,” he said. items.extracted_text: Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution - Artemis.bm Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution - Artemis.bm Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution 9th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Global Parametrics (part of CelsiusPro Group), has announced the development and planned pilot of Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance product, specifically designed to help protect 17,000 low-income household members against earthquake risk in Lima, Peru. The parametric product, which will be supported through the Natural Disaster Fund’s (NDF) Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) grant, will help safeguard livelihoods and mitigate the longer-term impact of earthquakes on employment and household incomes across Lima. The pilot aims to protect 5,000 vulnerable policyholders, supporting approximately 17,000 household members, primarily based in low-income and progressive housing. According to the announcement, this will lay the groundwork to scaling the product to up to 20,000 policyholders in its second year and for expansion beyond Lima. The product will initially have a key focus on Lima, where Global Parametrics, in partnership with MicroInsurance Centre at Milliman, Three Fin Consulting, Swisscontact, La Positiva Seguros and local microfinance institutions, will be able to work closely with local stakeholders, monitor implementation and assess the effectiveness of the product before scaling. Moreover, Global Parametrics explained that partnering with Swisscontact Peru supports a more holistic approach to resilience building, providing further support to progressive housing homeowners through risk reduction activities, including capacity building for local builders. Mark Rueegg, Founder and CEO of CelsiusPro Group, commented: “Delivering this pilot initiative in Peru marks the first signed NDF TAF grant contract signed since the replenishment of the TAF by the UK Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) announced in June. He continued: “Piloting this parametric insurance product against earthquake risk will demonstrate how innovative risk transfer solutions can provide greater financial stability for vulnerable households. By combining data with local expertise, we are developing practical solutions that can help close the protection gap and build greater resilience to natural hazards.” Peru is highly vulnerable to earthquake risk, as it lies in one of the world’s most seismically active regions along the convergent plate boundary between the Nazca and South American Plates. In addition, low-income households are especially vulnerable to the financial impacts of earthquakes. Having limited access to appropriate risk management tools, along with housing informality and the fact that the locations of many homes happen to be located in highly seismic areas can make it increasingly difficult for traditional insurers to provide affordable coverage for vulnerable households. As a result, this parametric solution being developed by the NDF will offer further ways to extend protection to these vulnerable households, including those without formal property titles. In addition, the parametric quake product will also be tailored to livelihood protection, recognising that the financial impact of an earthquake can extend beyond physical damage to homes and assets. By providing financial support following a qualifying seismic event, the solution aims to help households manage immediate costs and reduce the potential disruption to employment and household incomes. John Caroll, Consultant and Latin America Specialist for the MicroInsurance Centre, said: “We will integrate customercentric design at every stage of product development and piloting, incorporating input and validation from the target market throughout the process. We intend to engage in co-design approaches with our consortium partners. We are encouraged by our partners’ dedication in the lead-up to the pilot launch and are confident that, together, we can design a valuable and sustainable solution to protect low-income households and those living in progressive housing.” Swisscontact Chairman, Thomas Meyer, added: “Our partnership with Global Parametrics, alongside our Vivienda Progressiva (VIPRO) Program, will link insurance to our risk reduction programmes, combining financial resilience with measures designed to reduce exposure to earthquake risk. Peru is a vital location for this work: according to CENEPRED (2025), over 14.8 million people and 4.6 million homes face very high seismic risk. By combining financial protection with practical risk reduction measures, we can help vulnerable households and local communities prepare for and recover from the impact of earthquakes.” Lourdes del Carpio, Agrarian Insurance Manager at La Positiva Seguros, noted: “The evolution of the insurance sector depends on our ability to keep developing solutions that respond to the country’s changing protection needs. At La Positiva, we see innovation as an ongoing commitment to expanding the possibilities of insurance and reaching new segments. This initiative allows us to explore further applications of parametric insurance in Peru and contribute to the development of solutions tailored to the needs of families living in progressive housing.” The Natural Disaster Fund (NDF) was launched back in 2018 by Global Parametrics and was seeded by the UK’s Department for International Development (DFID) later on that same year.
